title: Rosenlicht splitting criterion for a solvable group dominated by a split torus
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field], and let $G$ be a smooth geometrically connected affine $k$-group scheme of finite type [def-sc-group-scheme, def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme, def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. Suppose $G$ is solvable in the group-scheme sense of [def-sfb-solvable-group-structure]: it has a finite descending series of closed subgroup schemes, normal in their predecessors, with commutative represented fppf quotients. Assume there is a $k$-morphism of schemes $f:(\mathbf G_{m,k})^N\to G$, for some integer $N\geq0$, whose image is dense in the underlying topological space. The morphism need not be a homomorphism. Then $G$ admits a finite series $G=G_0\supseteq\cdots\supseteq G_m=1$ of smooth geometrically connected closed $k$-subgroups [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup], each normal in its predecessor, with represented fppf quotients $G_i/G_{i+1}$ isomorphic to $\mathbf G_a$ or $\mathbf G_m$ [def-sc-gm-ga]. If $G$ is unipotent in the sense of [def-sfb-solvable-group-structure], all these quotients can be chosen isomorphic to $\mathbf G_a$. Here unipotence means existence of a faithful finite-dimensional closed matrix representation in which every geometric point differs nilpotently from the identity, and a represented fppf quotient has the meaning in [def-sfb-solvable-group-structure]. The empty series is permitted for $G=1$. There is no perfectness or characteristic restriction on $k$.

source.place: Theorem 16.58 (Rosenlicht), printed p.345; split solvable convention in Section 16g, p.343; splitness of the unipotent subgroup in Proposition 16.54 and its proof, p.344.

proof.text: For any smooth geometrically connected affine group $H$ occurring below, [lem-trf-smooth-connected-fibre-normal-integrality] makes $H$ geometrically integral. Thus its coordinate ring is a domain, and a dense morphism into $H$ has injective pullback: a function vanishing on the image vanishes at every prime, hence is nilpotent and therefore zero. If $\dim H=0$, [lem-pc-zero-dimensional-closed-subscheme-finite], applied to $H\hookrightarrow H$, makes $k[H]$ a finite-dimensional domain, hence a field (multiplication by a nonzero element is an injective endomorphism of a finite-dimensional vector space and is surjective). Evaluation at the identity embeds this field into $k$, identically on $k$, so $k[H]=k$ and $H=1$. In particular every nontrivial such $H$ has positive dimension.

source.place: Theorem 16.58, dimension induction; Corollary 5.26 and Propositions 1.34-1.35 for group-variety geometry.

proof.text: Split series are closed under extension in the precise form needed here. If $N\triangleleft H$ and $N,H,Q=H/N$ are smooth geometrically connected, take the inverse images in $H$ of the terms of a split series for $Q$, then append a split series for $N$. The correspondence and quotient clauses of [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry] identify each quotient in the lifted segment with the corresponding quotient for $Q$, and give closed normal inclusions. Its smoothness and connectedness clause, applied after every field extension, makes every inverse-image term smooth and geometrically connected. The appended terms already have these properties. The same argument gives additive-only series when both input series have additive-only quotients.

source.place: Section 16g, p.343: extensions of split solvable groups are split.

proof.text: First treat a smooth geometrically connected group $H$ of multiplicative type dominated by $f:T_0=\mathbf G_m^N\to H$. Replace $f$ by $h(t)=f(1)^{-1}f(t)$, so $h(1)=1$. Over $\bar k$, embed $H_{\bar k}$ in a power of $\mathbf G_m$ using the meaning of multiplicative type in [lem-sfb-unipotent-to-multiplicative-trivial]. For any coordinate unit $u$ of the composite, apply [lem-sfb-rosenlicht-product-unit-factorization] on $T_{0,\bar k}\times T_{0,\bar k}$ to $u(xy)$. The normalized identity reads $u(xy)=u(x)u(y)$, so the composite, and therefore $h_{\bar k}$, is a group homomorphism. Equality of the two coordinate pullbacks descends by injectivity in [lem-sfb-field-extension-tensor-injective]; hence $h$ is a homomorphism over $k$. Its closed-image factorization is [lem-sfb-affine-homomorphism-flat-image]. Density and reducedness of $H$ force the closed-image ideal to be zero, so $h$ is faithfully flat. By [lem-sfb-field-split-torus-flat-quotient], $H$ is a split torus. Its coordinate-factor series has successive quotients $\mathbf G_m$.

source.place: Theorem 16.58, first special case; Proposition 12.49, p.247; quotient of a split torus, p.236.

proof.text: Next let $H$ be a smooth geometrically connected closed subgroup of $\mathbf G_a^n$ in characteristic $p>0$, dominated by $f:\mathbf G_m^N\to H$. Put $A=k_\sigma[F]$, $\sigma(c)=c^p$, with multiplication as in [lem-sfb-primitive-frobenius-module-duality]. That node identifies $P(H)=\operatorname{Hom}(H,\mathbf G_a)$ with a finitely generated left $A$-module and reconstructs $H$ from it. By [lem-sfb-affine-group-coordinate-hopf], these homomorphisms are exactly primitive coordinate functions: the equality $a(xy)=a(x)+a(y)$ is $\Delta(a)=a\otimes1+1\otimes a$. A constant primitive is zero, since $c=2c$ implies $c=0$. Thus $P(H)\to k[H]/k$ is injective. Dominance gives an injective map $k[H]/k\to L/k$, where $L=k[z_1^{\pm1},\ldots,z_N^{\pm1}]$: if $f^*a=c$, injectivity of $f^*$ gives $a=c$. The composite is $A$-linear for $F[a]=[a^p]$; this action is well-defined modulo constants because $(a+c)^p-a^p=c^p$.

source.place: Theorem 16.58, elementary-unipotent case, p.345; Theorem 14.46, p.295.

proof.text: The left $A$-module $L/k$ is free. Index a basis by the vectors $v\in\mathbf Z^N\setminus\{0\}$ not in $p\mathbf Z^N$, sending the generator $e_v$ to $[z^v]$. Indeed each nonzero exponent $u$ has a unique expression $u=p^rv$ with $r\geq0$ and $v\notin p\mathbf Z^N$. For $\sum_r c_rF^r\in A$, its value on $[z^v]$ is $\sum_r c_r[z^{p^rv}]$. Distinct pairs $(v,r)$ give distinct Laurent monomials, so this map $\bigoplus_v A\to L/k$ is both injective and surjective, by coefficient comparison. This also covers $N=0$, when both sides are zero. Apply [lem-sfb-frobenius-skew-free-submodules] to the finitely generated image of $P(H)$ in this free module: $P(H)\simeq A^d$. Reconstruction by [lem-sfb-primitive-frobenius-module-duality] now gives $H\simeq\mathbf G_a^d$: an $A$-linear map $A^d\to R$ is uniquely determined by its $d$ basis values in $R$, with addition coordinatewise. Coordinate-factor subgroups give the desired additive series.

source.place: Theorem 16.58, Laurent-monomial argument, p.345; Proposition 14.50, p.296.

proof.text: In characteristic zero, let $H$ be commutative and smooth geometrically connected, still with a dominant torus morphism. The field is perfect, so [lem-sfb-perfect-commutative-torus-unipotent-product] gives $H\simeq U\times T$, with both factors smooth geometrically connected, $T$ a torus and $U$ closed in a unitriangular group. Projection of the dominant morphism onto $T$ is dominant (the projection is surjective and continuous), so step 3 splits $T$. The commutative factor $U$ is a vector group by [lem-sfb-char-zero-commutative-unipotent-vector-group]. The additive coordinate series of $U$, the multiplicative coordinate series of $T$, and step 2 therefore give the required split series of $H$.

source.place: Theorem 16.58, characteristic-zero commutative reduction; Theorem 16.13 and Corollary 16.15, pp.328-329; Corollary 14.33, p.289.

proof.text: We now prove the solvable conclusion by strong induction on $d=\dim G$, for every smooth geometrically connected solvable affine group with a dominant torus morphism. Step 1 handles $d=0$. For later reductions, a nontrivial proper smooth geometrically connected normal subgroup $N\subset G$ has $0<\dim N<d$: positivity is step 1 and strictness is [lem-wf-affine-dimension-drop], since $G$ is integral. The quotient $Q=G/N$ is smooth geometrically connected by [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry], and [lem-sfb-homogeneous-quotient-krull-dimension] gives $\dim Q=d-\dim N<d$. Whenever both $N$ and $Q$ have dominant torus morphisms and are solvable, the induction hypothesis splits each and step 2 splits $G$. This is the induction assertion used below, not an assumption that arbitrary subgroups inherit domination.

source.place: Theorem 16.58, general case: dimension induction, p.345.

proof.text: Take $D=D(G)$ from [lem-sfb-derived-commutator-word-arbitrary-field]. It and $G/D$ are smooth geometrically connected, and the quotient is commutative. Both are solvable: intersect a solvable series with $D$ and use that commutators in each intersection lie in the next; its commutative quotients are represented by [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry]. The quotient $G/D$ is commutative, hence solvable. Explicitly $D^i(G)$ lies in the $i$th term of the given subnormal series; if $D(G)=G$, all $D^i(G)=G$, forcing $G=1$. Thus for nontrivial $G$, $D\ne G$. If $D=1$, $G$ is commutative. Otherwise $D$ has a dominant torus morphism: compose the dominant word $w_r:G^{2r}\to D$ with $f^{2r}$. To check dominance, the tensor powers of the injective coordinate map $f^*$ remain injective by [lem-weil-pbc-module-over-field-flat, lem-trf-flat-tensor-preserves-injection], so $f^{2r}$ and then its composite with $w_r$ are dominant. The quotient $G/D$ is dominated by the composite of $f$ with its faithfully flat quotient map. Step 7 applies. It remains only to split commutative $G$; characteristic zero was settled in step 6.

source.place: Theorem 16.58, reduction by the derived group, p.345; Proposition 6.20(a), p.130.

proof.text: Suppose now $G$ is commutative and $\operatorname{char}k=p>0$. Factor $[p]_G:G\to G$ through its closed image $I$ using [lem-sfb-algebraic-group-homomorphism-factorization]. Its kernel $K$ is normal and the quotient description is $I=G/K$. Thus [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry] makes $I$ smooth geometrically connected. It is dominated by the torus through $G\to I$. The quotient $G/I$ is also smooth geometrically connected and dominated through $G\to G/I$. All these groups are commutative, hence solvable. If $1\ne I\ne G$, step 7 and the induction hypothesis apply to $I\triangleleft G$; step 2 finishes. If $I=1$, then $[p]_G=0$, and [lem-sfb-smooth-p-torsion-additive-embedding] embeds $G$ as a closed subgroup of a vector group over $k$. Steps 4-5 give $G\simeq\mathbf G_a^d$.

source.place: Theorem 16.58, positive-characteristic multiplication-by-p reduction, p.345; Proposition 14.49, p.296.

proof.text: In the remaining case $I=G$, the closed immersion $I\hookrightarrow G$ is an isomorphism ($I$ is smooth, hence reduced, and $G$ is reduced), so $[p]_G$ is flat and surjective on underlying spaces. Its coordinate map is a flat ring map (source and target are affine) inducing a surjection of prime spectra, hence faithfully flat in the sense of [def-weil-pbc-faithfully-flat-ring-map] by [lem-weil-pbc-flat-surjective-spectrum-faithfully-flat]. Over $F=\bar k$, apply [lem-sfb-commutative-diagonalizable-unipotent-product]: $G_F\simeq U\times D$ with $U\hookrightarrow\mathcal U_n$ and $D$ diagonalizable. Each factor is a quotient by the other and hence smooth and geometrically connected by [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry]. For $p^e\geq n$, every upper unitriangular matrix $1+X$ over every $F$-algebra satisfies $(1+X)^{p^e}=1+X^{p^e}=1$, since $X^n=0$. Thus $[p^e]_U=0$. On the other hand $[p^e]_{G_F}$ is faithfully flat: base change preserves faithful flatness [lem-weil-pbc-faithfully-flat-base-change]. Composition does too directly from [def-weil-pbc-faithfully-flat-ring-map]: for $R\to S\to B$, tensoring a complex with $B$ is tensoring first with $S$ and then with $B$ over $S$, and each functor preserves and reflects exactness. The projection $U\times_FD\to U$ is faithfully flat: its coordinate map $F[U]\to F[U]\otimes_FF[D]$ is the base change along $F\to F[U]$ of $F\to F[D]$, which is flat [lem-weil-pbc-module-over-field-flat] and surjective on spectra because $F[D]\neq0$, hence faithfully flat [lem-weil-pbc-flat-surjective-spectrum-faithfully-flat]; base change keeps it faithfully flat [lem-weil-pbc-faithfully-flat-base-change]. The composite $\operatorname{pr}_U\circ[p^e]_{G_F}$ is therefore faithfully flat, and it equals $[p^e]_U\circ\operatorname{pr}_U$, the constant homomorphism. Injectivity of its coordinate map [lem-weil-pbc-faithfully-flat-universally-injective], applied to the source ring as a module over itself, forces every $a\in F[U]$ to equal $\epsilon(a)$, so $U=1$. Thus $G_F\simeq D$ is diagonalizable and $G$ is of multiplicative type, exactly the geometric definition. Step 3 splits $G$. This completes the strong induction.

source.place: Theorem 16.58, case G=pG, p.345; Theorem 16.13(b), p.328. The geometric product argument avoids imposing perfection on k.

proof.text: Finally assume the original $G$ is unipotent and use the split series just obtained. Each smooth closed term $G_i$ is unipotent: restrict the faithful representation of $G$; the restriction is still a closed embedding and its geometric matrices remain unipotent. If a quotient $G_i/G_{i+1}$ in this series were $\mathbf G_m$, its quotient homomorphism would be trivial by [lem-sfb-unipotent-to-multiplicative-trivial], contradicting its faithful flatness onto the nontrivial multiplicative group. Thus every quotient is $\mathbf G_a$. All terms are smooth geometrically connected and all quotient maps represent the fppf quotients by construction. The group $1$ admits the empty series, also covering a dominant morphism with $N=0$.

source.place: Split conventions, Section 16g, p.343 and Definition 14.61, p.299; unipotent-to-multiplicative vanishing, Corollary 14.18(a), p.284.

Steps 1-11: I checked each against the statement of every node it cites and against Milne. Step 3 (multiplicative type): the unit-factorization node over k̄ makes the translated map a homomorphism; it descends to k, and faithful flatness of its image then gives a split torus (in place of Milne's 12.49). Steps 4-5: primitive-Frobenius duality and the Laurent-monomial basis v∉pZ^N, which is Milne's condition Zp+ΣZr_i=Z. Step 6: characteristic zero, by the perfect-field product and the vector-group node. Step 7: an explicit strong induction on dimension. Step 8: derived reduction; I checked that the derived terms sit inside the given series (D^i⊆G_i) and that the dominant commutator word stays dominant through the tensor power of f. Steps 9-10: factor [p]_G through its image; G=pG is handled by a geometric product argument over k̄, so k need not be perfect. Step 11: the unipotent clause. New nodes, all true, statement-only and not duplicates: (1) derived-commutator-word, from Milne 6.18-6.21; the existing derived-subgroup and word-kernel nodes work only over algebraically closed fields. (2) frobenius-skew-free-submodules: the right division algorithm (Milne p.296) needs no perfection, and 14.50 then applies; the existing left-principal node gives only finite generation, the division node assumes σ is an automorphism, and the cyclic-decomposition node assumes k perfect. (3) perfect-commutative-torus-unipotent-product, from Milne 16.13(b), 16.15 and 14.5; the existing product node works only over k̄ with factors that need not be smooth.
